questions.prompt: Which group axiom says that \(a*b\in G\) whenever \(a,b\in G\)?
questions.answer: This is the closure axiom. It says the operation never takes two elements of the set and produces an output outside the set.

questions.prompt: Write the associativity axiom for a binary operation \(*\).
questions.answer: Associativity is \((a*b)*c=a*(b*c)\) for all \(a,b,c\in G\). It says the grouping of a threefold product does not change the result.

questions.prompt: For multiplication on \(\{1,-1\}\), what is the identity element?
questions.answer: The identity is \(1\), because \(1\cdot1=1\), \(1\cdot(-1)=-1\), and multiplying on the other side by \(1\) also leaves each element unchanged.

questions.prompt: For multiplication on \(\{1,-1\}\), what is the inverse of \(-1\)?
questions.answer: The inverse of \(-1\) is \(-1\) itself, because \((-1)(-1)=1\), and \(1\) is the identity element.

questions.prompt: Show that \(\{1,-1\}\) is closed under multiplication.
questions.answer: Check all products: \(1\cdot1=1\), \(1\cdot(-1)=-1\), \((-1)\cdot1=-1\), and \((-1)(-1)=1\). Every result is in \(\{1,-1\}\), so closure holds.

questions.prompt: For \(G=\{0,1\}\) under addition modulo \(2\), list the inverse of each element.
questions.answer: The identity is \(0\). The inverse of \(0\) is \(0\), because \(0+0\equiv0\pmod2\). The inverse of \(1\) is \(1\), because \(1+1\equiv0\pmod2\).

questions.prompt: Why does one successful example of closure not prove the closure axiom for an infinite set?
questions.answer: Closure must hold for every pair of elements in the set. One example only shows that one chosen pair works. For an infinite set, a proof must use arbitrary elements \(a,b\) or a general argument covering all possible pairs.

questions.prompt: A set has a left identity \(e*a=a\) for every \(a\). Is that alone enough for the identity axiom?
questions.answer: No. The identity axiom requires a two-sided identity: \(e*a=a\) and \(a*e=a\) for every \(a\). If only the left equation is known, the right equation must still be checked.

questions.prompt: Test associativity for subtraction using \(a=8\), \(b=3\), and \(c=2\).
questions.answer: Compute the two groupings. \((8-3)-2=5-2=3\). But \(8-(3-2)=8-1=7\). Since \(3\ne7\), subtraction is not associative.

questions.prompt: Show that the odd integers are not closed under addition.
questions.answer: Choose two odd integers, for example \(1\) and \(3\). Their sum is \(1+3=4\), which is even and not odd. Since a product of two elements of the set leaves the set, closure under addition fails.

questions.prompt: For the integers under addition, verify the inverse axiom for an arbitrary integer \(a\).
questions.answer: The identity is \(0\). For any integer \(a\), the integer \(-a\) also lies in \(\mathbb Z\). Then \(a+(-a)=0\) and \((-a)+a=0\). Therefore every integer has an additive inverse in the set.

questions.prompt: Explain why associativity for \(\{1,-1\}\) under multiplication can be inherited from real multiplication.
questions.answer: The operation is ordinary multiplication restricted to the subset \(\{1,-1\}\). Real multiplication is associative for all real numbers, so \((ab)c=a(bc)\) holds in particular when \(a,b,c\) are chosen from \(\{1,-1\}\).

questions.prompt: Check all four group axioms for \(\{1,-1,i,-i\}\) under complex multiplication.
questions.answer: Closure holds because products of fourth roots of unity remain in the set. Associativity is inherited from complex multiplication. The identity is \(1\). Inverses are \(1^{-1}=1\), \((-1)^{-1}=-1\), \(i^{-1}=-i\), and \((-i)^{-1}=i\). Hence the set is a group.

questions.prompt: The set \(\{0,1,2,3\}\) uses addition modulo \(4\). Verify that every element has an inverse.
questions.answer: The identity is \(0\). The inverse of \(0\) is \(0\). The inverse of \(1\) is \(3\), since \(1+3\equiv0\pmod4\). The inverse of \(2\) is \(2\), since \(2+2\equiv0\pmod4\). The inverse of \(3\) is \(1\). All inverses are in the set.

questions.prompt: A binary operation on \(G\) has a table whose entries all lie in \(G\). Which axiom is proved, and which axioms remain?
questions.answer: The table proves closure, because every product listed is an element of \(G\). Associativity still needs triple-product checks, an identity element must be found and checked on both sides, and each element must have a two-sided inverse in \(G\).

questions.prompt: Suppose \(e\) is an identity and \(a*b=e\). Why is this not always enough to prove \(b\) is the inverse of \(a\)?
questions.answer: A group inverse must be two-sided: \(a*b=e\) and \(b*a=e\). The equation \(a*b=e\) only shows that \(b\) is a right inverse for \(a\). Unless commutativity or another argument gives \(b*a=e\), the inverse axiom has not been fully checked.

questions.prompt: For \(G=\mathbb R\) with \(a*b=a+b+ab\), show why \(-1\) causes the inverse axiom to fail on all real numbers.
questions.answer: First find the identity: \(a*e=a\) gives \(a+e+ae=a\), so \(e(1+a)=0\) for all \(a\), hence \(e=0\). An inverse \(x\) for \(-1\) would satisfy \((-1)*x=0\). But \(-1+x-x=-1\), never \(0\). Thus \(-1\) has no inverse, so all real numbers do not form a group under this operation.

questions.prompt: Give a proof that closure and inverses imply the identity lies in a non-empty subgroup candidate \(H\) of a group \(G\).
questions.answer: Choose any \(h\in H\), possible because \(H\) is non-empty. If \(H\) is closed under inverses, then \(h^{-1}\in H\). If \(H\) is closed under products, then \(h*h^{-1}\in H\). But in \(G\), \(h*h^{-1}=e\). Therefore \(e\in H\).

questions.prompt: A student checks closure, identity, and inverses for a new operation, then says associativity is obvious because the operation is commutative. Diagnose the error.
questions.answer: Commutativity and associativity are different statements. Commutativity says \(a*b=b*a\). Associativity says \((a*b)*c=a*(b*c)\). Switching order does not justify moving parentheses, so associativity must be proved or inherited from a known associative operation.

questions.prompt: Why is finding a different identity-like element for each \(a\in G\) not enough for the identity axiom?
questions.answer: The identity axiom requires one fixed element \(e\in G\) such that \(e*a=a*e=a\) for every \(a\in G\). If the element changes with \(a\), then there is no single do-nothing element for the whole structure, so the group definition is not satisfied.
